title: जलवायु परिवर्तन का मंडरा रहा खतरा, 1.5 डिग्री तापमान वृद्धि की दहलीज पर दुनिया - Jagran
search_term: ("पारा चढ़ा" OR "पारा पहुंचा" OR तापमान OR "तापमान बढ़ा" OR "रिकॉर्ड तोड़ गर्मी" OR "डिग्री सेल्सियस" OR "पारा उबला" OR "अधिकतम तापमान" OR "तापमान 40 पार" OR "तापमान 45 पार" OR "तापमान बढ़ने की संभावना") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
full_text:
जलवायु परिवर्तन का मंडरा रहा खतरा, 1.5 डिग्री तापमान वृद्धि की दहलीज पर दुनिया
एक नए अध्ययन के अनुसार, पृथ्वी औद्योगिक युग से पहले के स्तर की तुलना में 2025 के अंत तक लगभग 1.5 डिग्री सेल्सियस गर्म हो चुकी है।
समय कम है?
जानिए मुख्य बातें और खबर का सार एक नजर में
डिजिटल डेस्क, नई दिल्ली। जलवायु परिवर्तन का खतरा अब भविष्य की चिंता नहीं, बल्कि आज की हकीकत बन चुका है। वैश्विक तापमान में बढ़ोतरी अब उस स्तर के बेहद करीब पहुंच गई है, जिसे विज्ञानी जलवायु संकट का अहम पड़ाव मानते हैं।
नए अध्ययन के मुताबिक लगभग पूरी धरती औद्योगिक युग से पहले के स्तर की तुलना में लगभग 1.5 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक (90 से 94 प्रतिशत) तक वर्ष 2025 के अंत में ही गर्म हो गई थी।
धरती 2025 के अंत तक 1.5 डिग्री सेल्सियस गर्म हुई
इसका मतलब है कि दुनिया के कई हिस्से पहले ही उस तापमान के बेहद करीब पहुंच चुके हैं, जिसे पार करने से बचने के लिए वैश्विक प्रयास किए जा रहे हैं। गौरतलब है कि करीब 200 देशों ने 2015 में पेरिस समझौता अपनाया था।
इसका उद्देश्य यह सुनिश्चित करना था कि जलवायु परिवर्तन के सबसे गंभीर प्रभावों से बचने के लिए वैश्विक तापमान वृद्धि को औद्योगिक युग से पहले के स्तर की तुलना में 1.5 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक नहीं बढ़ने दिया जाए।
नेचर क्लाइमेट चेंज पत्रिका में प्रकाशित इस अध्ययन में औद्योगिक युग से पहले के समय की तुलना में दुनिया के अलग-अलग क्षेत्रों में तापमान वृद्धि का आकलन किया गया है।
कनाडा के यूनिवर्सिटी आफ विक्टोरिया के पैसिफिक क्लाइमेट इम्पैक्ट्स कंसोर्टियम के शोधकर्ता टोंग ली ने कहा कि क्षेत्रीय स्तर पर भी मौजूदा तापमान वृद्धि 1.5 डिग्री वाली स्थिति के करीब पहुंच चुकी है। ऐसे में सभी क्षेत्रों को जलवायु परिवर्तन के प्रभावों से निपटने की तैयारी करनी होगी।
पेरिस समझौते का 1.5 डिग्री लक्ष्य खतरे में पड़ गया
अध्ययन के अनुसार, इंसानी गतिविधियों के कारण दुनिया के जमीन वाले हिस्सों का औसत तापमान औद्योगिक युग से पहले की तुलना में करीब 1.9 डिग्री सेल्सियस बढ़ चुका है। जमीन का तापमान समुद्र के मुकाबले तेजी से बढ़ता है। इसका असर खासतौर पर उत्तरी ध्रुव के आसपास के इलाकों में ज्यादा दिखाई दे रहा है।
यह अध्ययन ऐसे समय आया है जब दुनियाभर के नेता, नीति-निर्माता और शोधकर्ता सोमवार से तुर्किये के अंताल्या में शुरू हो रहे संयुक्त राष्ट्र जलवायु परिवर्तन सम्मेलन यानी सीओपी31 के लिए जुट रहे हैं।
जलवायु परिवर्तन के प्रभाव अब वर्तमान की हकीकत
पैसिफिक क्लाइमेट इम्पैक्ट्स कंसोर्टियम के सांख्यिकीविद् विज्ञानी फ्रांसिस ज्वियर्स ने कहा, 1.5 डिग्री सेल्सियस तापवृद्धि से जुड़े जलवायु जोखिम अब भविष्य की चिंता नहीं रह गए हैं; दुनियाभर में लोग पहले से ही इनका अनुभव कर रहे हैं।
हम ऐसी जानकारी उपलब्ध करा रहे हैं, जिसका इस्तेमाल अलग-अलग क्षेत्रों के नीति निर्माता और निर्णय लेने वाले यह आकलन करने के लिए कर सकेंगे कि उनके क्षेत्र किस हद तक प्रभावित हो रहे हैं।
उत्तर-पश्चिमी उत्तरी अमेरिका में तापमान वृद्धि तीन डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच गई है, जबकि मेक्सिको सहित मध्य अमेरिका के उत्तरी हिस्से में यह करीब 1.7 डिग्री रही। कनाडा में पिछले दशक के दौरान तापमान औद्योगिक युग से पहले के स्तर के मुकाबले 2.2 डिग्री अधिक दर्ज किया गया।
शोधकर्ताओं के मुताबिक, दुनिया के अलग-अलग क्षेत्रों में तापमान बढ़ने की रफ्तार भले ही अलग हो, लेकिन सभी क्षेत्र लगभग 2029 तक 1.5 डिग्री ग्लोबल वार्मिंग के बराबर क्षेत्रीय तापमान वृद्धि के स्तर पर पहुंच सकते हैं।

title: Deep Reefs Offer Corals Little Refuge From Extreme Heat - Mirage News

full_text:
Once regarded as potential safe havens for corals in a warming climate, deep reefs, which inhabit depths between 90 and 150 meters (295 and 490 feet), are no longer sheltered from increasingly intense marine heatwaves, according to a new study.
Marine heatwaves increase the chances of disrupting the tiny algae that live within corals, leading to coral bleaching and even mass die-off events. As human activities continue to raise global temperatures, the growing intensity of marine heatwaves at depth may leave tropical corals without cooler waters to retreat to, threatening biodiversity, fisheries, and tourism throughout reef regions.
"Ocean warming is not just a surface problem. What happens deep beneath the surface can also have serious consequences for coral reef survival," said Chunzai Wang, an oceanographer at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and co-author of the study.
The study appears in Geophysical Research Letters, AGU's journal for high-impact, innovative, and timely articles on major advances across all major geoscience disciplines.
Peering beneath the surface
Scientists have proposed using deep reefs as "seed banks" - transplant sites for reproduction-ready corals from suffering shallow reefs. But "going deeper does not necessarily mean escaping the heat," Wang said.
To understand how marine heatwaves affect reefs beyond the top 30 meters (98 feet) of the ocean, researchers used global maps of warm-water coral reefs to filter ocean-wide simulations of daily water temperatures down to 150 meters (490 feet) from 1993 to 2023. These warm reefs occur around the world within 35 degrees of the equator, at latitudes roughly between Santa Barbara, California and Adelaide, Australia.
The simulated water temperatures use ocean circulation patterns and physics to fill the gaps between real measurements, creating a more complete record of reef heatwaves than is available from satellite measurements which can only see surface temperatures. With this deeper view of reef heat exposure, researchers tracked the number, durations and temperatures of marine heatwaves, which oceanographers define as a stretch of at least five days with seawater warmer than 90% of the historical temperatures recorded for that time of year.
The team also calculated heatwave "intensity," a metric that accounts for both temperature and duration. According to NOAA, corals risk bleaching once they've been received four "degree-weeks" of heat - the equivalent of four weeks at 1 C above normal temperatures, or a commensurately shorter time at higher temperatures (for example, two weeks at 2 C hotter, or just one week at 4 C hotter).
Deep reefs' demise
Deep reefs may still have been plausible coral refuges prior to 2010, the researchers suggested. Before this date, marine heatwaves typically impacted less than 50% of global reef areas per year, largely sparing deeper reefs from sustained high temperatures. Between 1993 and 2010, the average deep reef heatwave lasted less than 15 days except for during the 1997-1998 El Niño.
From 2010 onwards, however, heatwaves hit over half of the world's tropical reefs in 8 of the 13 years studied - roughly four times more often than in the preceding 17 years. The average heatwave in reefs over 90 meters (295 feet) below the surface stretched to 15 or more days in all but two years, typically bringing temperatures around 2 C higher than normal.
The worst coral conditions seen in the study came from three back-to-back La Niña events. Between 2020 and 2023, strong westward winds over the Pacific year after year built up an unusually deep-reaching pool of warm water in the western Pacific, ramping up global marine heatwaves beyond any other events since 1993. At their peak, the 2020-2023 marine heatwaves impacted over 75% of global tropical coral reefs areas at all depths.
Coral Conservation
Although marine heatwaves at depth occurred less frequently than those at the surface throughout the study period, their increased duration after 2010 has made them more intense, on average, than those in shallower waters. According to researchers, this could scupper hopes of shelter for corals during the extreme ocean heat events on the rise due to human-caused climate change.
The most important intervention for protecting corals is limiting global warming from human actions. "Local conservation measures can help reefs withstand environmental stress, but they cannot fully protect coral ecosystems from increasingly widespread ocean heat extremes," Wang said.

title: Orange alert weather warning issued for parts of Vancouver Island - CHEK News
search_term: ("heat advisory" OR "heat action plan" OR "heat alert" OR "IMD warning" OR "IMD alert" OR "red alert" OR "orange alert" OR "yellow alert" OR "NDMA advisory" OR "cooling shelter" OR "relief measures" OR "heat compensation" OR "severe weather warning") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
full_text:
Weather warnings are blanketing most of Vancouver Island on Tuesday, including two “orange alert” rainfall warnings where totals could reach 250 millimetres over the next two days.
An orange level rainfall warning is in effect for West and Inland Vancouver Island, where Environment Canada is predicting 150 to 200 millimetres of rain to fall from Tuesday morning through Thursday morning – with some areas potentially seeing more than 250 millimetres locally.
The rain is expected to ease Wednesday afternoon but continue through Thursday before another weather system arrives on Vancouver Island on Friday, according to Environment Canada.
“Localized flooding is likely. Some roads may become impassable. Visibility will likely be suddenly reduced at times,” said the weather office. “Landslides may occur in vulnerable areas such as steep slopes, deforested areas or recent burn scars.”
More yellow weather alerts for Vancouver Island
Meanwhile, in East Vancouver Island, a yellow alert rainfall warning and a wind warning are in effect, from Nanoose Bay to Campbell River.
Here, 50 to 100 millimetres of rain is expected to fall from Tuesday morning through Wednesday night, while southeast wind gusts of 70 km/h to 90 km/h are expected to blow through from Tuesday afternoon into Wednesday morning.
In North Vancouver Island, yellow alerts for rain and wind are also in effect Tuesday.
Some 100 milimetres of rain is expected to fall Tuesday, with the heaviest rain developing in the afternoon and continuing until Wednesday morning – particularly in the areas of Port Alice, Woss and Quatsino.
Southeasterly wind gusts of 90 km/h to 110 km/h are also expected to develop late Tuesday afternoon and continue through the late evening for the North Island.
Last year, Environment Canada introduced a new colour-coded weather alert system, with yellow being the least severe, followed by orange and red alerts.
A yellow alert is described as the most common type of weather warning with impacts “likely moderate, localized, and/or short term,” according to the federal government.
An orange alert is described as severe damage that is likely to cause “significant damage” or disruption and pose a greater risk of injury. “Impacts can be major, widespread, and/or may last a few days,” reads the Environment Canada website.
Red alerts will be rare, and will only be issued when “very dangerous and possibly life-threatening weather will cause extreme damage and disruption.”
As of Monday afternoon, flood watches were in effect for almost all areas of Vancouver Island – including North, West, Central and East Vancouver Island, according to the BC River Forecast Centre.
A flood watch means river levels are rising and could exceed their riverbanks. It is more severe than a high streamflow advisory, but lower than a flood warning.
“Heavy rain and high streamflow bring increased risk for unstable banks, river erosion, submerged roads, swift water hazards, flooding and landslides,” said the forecast centre. “Stay clear of the banks of swift-running rivers and never drive across flooded roads, bridges or river crossings.”
It also asked for people to keep storm drains clear of leaves and other debris to help reduce flooding.

title: Orange alert: Storm Charles hits Gran Canaria - Teneriffa News
search_term: ("heat advisory" OR "heat action plan" OR "heat alert" OR "IMD warning" OR "IMD alert" OR "red alert" OR "orange alert" OR "yellow alert" OR "NDMA advisory" OR "cooling shelter" OR "relief measures" OR "heat compensation" OR "severe weather warning") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
full_text:
The president of the Gran Canaria Island Council, Antonio Morales, has urged the public to exercise caution in the face of the new ‚high-impact‘ storm, Charles, which is set to affect the island from this afternoon and evening until Wednesday night, particularly in the summit area and in the north-west and south-east.
Antonio Morales, the Regional Minister for the Environment, Raúl García Brink, and emergency services officer Federico Grillo have reported on this «high-impact» phenomenon, which will keep Gran Canaria on orange alert for winds and coastal events and on yellow alert for rain; in response, the Island Council will deploy 1,000 personnel to deal with any incidents that may arise.
The Canary Islands Government, with which the Island Council has held a meeting, has issued a warning for strong winds and coastal phenomena in Gran Canaria, as gusts of up to 90 kilometres per hour are expected, which may occasionally exceed 100 kilometres per hour, Mr Morales said.
Gran Canaria: Storm Charles brings rain and the risk of landslides
Rainfall is initially not expected to be significant, with isolated showers associated with storms forecast; a pre-alert has therefore been issued, although he has emphasised the need to monitor the storm’s development closely.
The Island Council will meet with the local councils and officials from the Regional Ministry of Public Works and the Island Water Board ahead of the arrival of the storm, which appears set to last for less time than originally forecast, according to Morales, who has urged motorists to drive with caution due to the risk of landslides and falling trees, amongst other possible consequences.
Gran Canaria has no plans to introduce any restrictions at present
According to Morales, the storm will be less severe in the capital of Gran Canaria than in other parts of the island.
Similarly, no restrictions of any kind are currently planned, such as those introduced last Sunday during Storm Bruna, when the Island Council agreed to suspend all activities at public and private centres across the island.
